<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Coping with the onslaught of kernel security bugs</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096908/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096908/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>By now it is no secret that large language models (LLMs) have made it easy
for people to identify security bugs, and that has resulted in a flood of
bug reports to almost every free-software project, including the kernel.
At the 2026 edition of <a href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel
Recipes</a>, Greg Kroah-Hartman took the stage to talk about how the
kernel's security team is handling this deluge.  His core message was
"<q>don't panic</q>".
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Beyond the &</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096028/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096028/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Rust has a number of kinds of smart pointers, both in the standard
library and defined by users. Still, some operations that are possible with
built-in references are not possible to perform with user-defined smart
pointers. Tyler Mandry, lead of the Rust project's
<a href="https://rust-lang.org/governance/teams/#team-lang">
language team</a>, spoke at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf 2026</a> about the lengthy effort to change that, and make smart pointers
just as flexible as built-in references.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>An update on the Sashiko patch-review system</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096963/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096963/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Patch review has long been one of the limiting constraints for the kernel
project (and most others); there just aren't enough people to properly
review all of the code that is submitted for inclusion.  The Sashiko
system, which uses a large language model (LLM) to generate reviews
automatically, offers the prospect of some relief, and has already become
an important part of the kernel's development process.  At the 2026 edition
of <a href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel Recipes</a>, Roman
Gushchin, the maintainer of Sashiko, provided an overview of how
the system works and what is being done to improve it.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Python's two modules for random numbers</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097468/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097468/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>Python's <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html"><tt>random</tt></a>
and <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3/library/secrets.html"><tt>secrets</tt></a>
modules both include utilities for obtaining random values, but only one of them is suitable for generating passwords and security tokens.
For much of Python's history, <tt>random</tt> was used for passwords and tokens anyway, despite documentation that called it unsuitable for cryptography.
In 2015, Python's core team debated whether to fix that misuse by making <tt>random</tt> secure by default.
Instead, in 2016, Python 3.6 added a second module: <tt>secrets</tt>.  The
<tt>random</tt> module is still misused at times, so it is instructive
to look into how the random-number modules should be used.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Last rites for Gentoo's Chromium package</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097760/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097760/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://www.chromium.org/Home/">Chromium</a>, the open-source
upstream project for Google's Chrome web browser, is the browser of choice for
many Linux users. It has also gained a reputation as being <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/619158/">difficult for Linux distributions to
package and build</a>: Chromium has a complex build system, the project bundles
many of its dependencies, and it has frequent releases. All of that, plus user
complaints, has led the maintainers of the <a
href="https://packages.gentoo.org/packages/www-client/chromium">Gentoo Chromium
package</a> to give up on trying to maintain the package.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Evolving the LAVD scheduler from gaming to servers</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097209/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097209/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/922405/">extensible scheduler class</a>, which
enables the creation of custom CPU schedulers with BPF, has led to a burst
of innovation in this area; <a
href="https://github.com/sched-ext/scx/tree/main/scheds/rust/scx_lavd#scx_lavd">the
LAVD scheduler</a> has, perhaps, been one of the most noteworthy schedulers
to emerge.  Though it was originally <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1051430/">designed
for gaming applications</a>, the LAVD scheduler has since grown to serve
other types of workloads as well.  At the 2026 edition of <a
href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel Recipes</a>, Changwoo Min
and Gavin Guo presented an overview of this scheduler and how it has
evolved over time.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Analyzing Rust programs with Charon</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097198/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1097198/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Nadrieril is a long-time Rust contributor, and the maintainer of the rustc
pattern-matching infrastructure. During his involvement with Rust, he has
noticed a problem with the usability of the language: it is difficult to
automatically extract information from a Rust crate for use with other tooling.
<a href="https://github.com/AeneasVerif/charon#charon">
The Charon project</a> aims to fix that by providing a stable API for accessing
internal information from the Rust compiler.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>An update on Rust's project goals</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098617/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098617/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Tomáš Šedovič is a program manager at the Rust Foundation. He co-leads the
<a href="https://rust-lang.org/governance/teams/#team-goals">
goals team</a>, which helps
organize the Rust project's
<a href="https://goals.rust-lang.org/2026/goals.html">
overall goals</a>, including making sure that the people
who have agreed to work on one have the support they need.
At Kangrejos 2026, he provided an overview of the Rust project's goal processes
aimed at ensuring that the Rust for Linux developers were aware of how the
project organizes, tracks, and amends goals.
The
<a href="https://rust-for-linux.com/">
Rust for Linux project</a>
has inspired several current project goals, so he thought that getting an inside
view of the process might be helpful.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The [vx]swap showdown</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098399/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098399/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The kernel's swap layer has undergone <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1057102/">some
significant changes</a> over the course of the last year and a number of
longstanding problems have been addressed.  One problem that has <i>not</i>
yet been solved in the mainline is the direct tie between slots in the swap
cache and space in persistent swap files, which can cause highly
inefficient resource use.  There are two competing solutions for this
problem, neither of which has, as yet, reached readiness for merging; a
lengthy discussion on possible paths forward shows ongoing disagreement
over the best path forward.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Adding kernel control-flow-integrity checking to GCC</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098670/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098670/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>While many developers are struggling to keep up with the flood of
vulnerability reports, others are still focused on preventing those reports
from happening in the first place.  Control-flow integrity (CFI) is the
term for preventing (or at least detecting) exploits that divert the flow
of control from its intended paths.  At the 2026 <a
href="https://gnu-tools-cauldron.org/">GNU Tools Cauldron</a>, Kees Cook
presented his changes to the GCC compiler suite to support forward-edge CFI
for the kernel.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The state of systemd: 2026 edition</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099024/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099024/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>At the 2026 <a href="https://all-systems-go.io/">All Systems Go!</a>
conference, systemd maintainers Luca Boccassi and Zbigniew Jędrzejewski-Szmek
delivered the traditional "state of the project" session with an overview of the
systemd project's accomplishments in the past year. That was followed by a
maintainer round table where Boccassi, Jędrzejewski-Szmek, Daan De&#160;Meyer, and
project leader Lennart Poettering fielded questions about systemd's size,
health, and if it might replace Kubernetes. (It will not.)</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
